verdicts.basis: The classifier's claim is 'no observable difference on ANY input' — that categorical claim is false, so EQUIVALENT cannot stand under owner directive #1. Mechanism: `A or {}` evaluates bool(A) at the `or`, then `if needles:` (L238) evaluates bool(needles) AGAIN; when A is truthy that is a SECOND bool(A) call on the same object. The mutant `{} or A` evaluates bool({}) (False) and assigns needles=A WITHOUT calling bool(A), so bool(A) is called only once, at L238. For any A with a non-idempotent __bool__ the two forms branch differently. Concrete distinguishing input: self.kw['needles'] = a dict subclass F = {'BC-1': ['XYZ']} whose __bool__ returns True on the 1st call and False thereafter, with background_text/rule_text containing 'XYZ'. ORIGINAL: L237 `F or {}` -> bool(F)#1=True -> needles=F; L238 `if needles:` -> bool(F)#2=False -> branch SKIPPED, no scan, _ocr proceeds to write rule/background and run OCR. MUTANT: L237 `{} or F` -> needles=F (no bool(F) call); L238 `if needles:` -> bool(F)#1=True -> branch ENTERED -> tripwire.scan_text finds 'XYZ' -> `if found:` -> raise CapabilityUnrunnable(tripwire.refusal(...)). Observable divergence: mutant raises CapabilityUnrunnable, original does not. A test driving _ocr (via session_kw) with such a needles object and asserting raises-vs-not kills the mutant. For all realistic needles (plain dict / None / absent, i.e. idempotent __bool__) the two forms are indeed indistinguishable (the differing value only occurs when A is falsy, where `if needles:` is False in both and needles is never read after L239) — so this is a narrow, contrived distinguisher — but it exists and is constructible, which defeats the 'no test can kill it on any input' basis. Per the binding rule (uphold EQUIVALENT only if confident NO input distinguishes; refute when in doubt), verdict is SURVIVED, not EQUIVALENT.
